problem:
If $C$ is a $4\times 4$ matrix and $\text{rank}(C+3I)=2,$ which of the following statements are true?

- $\text{Null}(C+3I)={0}$
- $C+3I$ is singular
- $\lambda =-3$ is an eigenvalue of $C$

activity_context.topic_title: The Invertible Matrix Theorem in Terms of Eigenvalues

feedback.problem:
If $C$ is a $2\times 2$ matrix and $\text{nullity}(C-2I)=1,$ which of the following statements are true?

- $\text{Col}(C-2I)={R}^{2}$
- $C-2I$ is non-singular
- $\lambda =2$ is an eigenvalue of $C$
feedback.worked_solution:
Given a $2\times 2$ matrix $M,$ we have the following by the invertible matrix theorem:

$M$ is invertible $\,⇔\,{\,\begin{aligned} & \text{Col}(M)={R}^{2} \\  & \text{dim(Col}(M))=2=\text{rank}(M) \\  & \text{Null}(M)={0} \\  & \text{dim(Null}(M))=0=\text{nullity}(M)\end{aligned}$

Also, according to the rank-nullity theorem, if $M$ has $2$ columns, then 

$$
\text{rank}(M)+\text{nullity}(M)=2.
$$

With that in mind, let's examine our statements in turn.

- Statement I is false. According to the rank-nullity theorem, 

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{rank}(C-2I) & =2-\text{nullity}(C-2I) \\  & =2-1 \\  & =1.\end{aligned}
$$

As a result, $\text{Col}(C-2I)\ne {R}^{2}.$

- Statements II is false. By the invertible matrix theorem, since $\text{nullity}(C-2I)\ne 0,$ we obtain that $C-2I$ must be singular.

- Statement III is true. Notice that if $M=C-2I$ is singular, then $(C-2I)x=0$ has nonzero solutions which will be eigenvectors of $C.$ As a result, $\lambda =2$ is an eigenvalue of $C.$

Therefore, the correct answer is "III only."
